intro.description: Why the Laws of UX matter to Product, Engineering and QA, and how the training is structured

m1.description: Module 1 — How people decide: cognitive load, memory and choice (Hick’s Law worked example)

co.description: Choice Overload: too many options and people choose nothing

cl.description: Cognitive Load: spend people’s effort on the task, not the interface

wm.description: Working Memory: people hold about four things at once

ml.description: Miller’s Law: a warning about memory, not a rule about menus

ch.description: Chunking: group information so it can be scanned and recalled

sa.description: Selective Attention: people see what fits their goal

m1r.description: Module 1 recap and what comes next

m2.description: Module 2 — How people see: Gestalt grouping, contrast and beauty

px.description: Law of Proximity: space groups things

cr.description: Law of Common Region: a shared container makes a unit

si.description: Law of Similarity: things that look alike should act alike

uc.description: Uniform Connectedness: lines link things more strongly than space or color

pr.description: Law of Prägnanz: people see the simplest shape

vr.description: Von Restorff Effect: the one that differs gets remembered

m2r.description: Module 2 recap and what comes next

m3.description: Module 3 — How people act: targets, speed, input, focus and learning

fl.description: Fitts’s Law: big, close targets are faster to hit

dt.description: Doherty Threshold: respond in under about 400 ms

po.description: Postel’s Law: accept messy input, send clean output

fw.description: Flow: protect focus, match challenge to skill

pa.description: Paradox of the Active User: people skip the manual

m3r.description: Module 3 recap and what comes next

m4.description: Module 4 — How people expect and remember: conventions, models, memory and bias

jk.description: Jakob’s Law: people expect your product to work like the others

mm.description: Mental Model: people act on their picture of how it works

sp.description: Serial Position Effect: first and last are remembered

pe.description: Peak-End Rule: the peak and the ending define the memory

gg.description: Goal-Gradient Effect: effort rises near the goal

cb.description: Cognitive Bias: predictable shortcuts in judgment

m4r.description: Module 4 recap and what comes next

m5.description: Module 5 — How teams make trade-offs: complexity, simplicity, focus and time

tl.description: Tesler’s Law: complexity can’t vanish, only move

oc.description: Occam’s Razor: prefer the simplest option that works

pp.description: Pareto Principle: a vital few causes drive most effects

pk.description: Parkinson’s Law: tasks expand to fill the time

m5r.description: Module 5 recap and the close of the training
